title.after: Whether `/setup-web` also writes a headless browser server
title.before: Decide whether /setup-web also writes a headless browser server

messages.text: Title names the decision in plain words.

options.label: A
options.text: `/setup-web` writes both servers by default, the headless one with `--headless --isolated` alone, each under the same merge rules, and its report says when to use each: every project gets a second server to approve and load.

options.label: B
options.text: `/setup-web` writes the headless server only when the owner passes an argument such as `--headless`: a project must know to ask.

options.label: C
options.text: `/setup-web` stays headed-only, and its report says how to add a headless server by hand: two sessions in one project still contend for the browser.

problem:
`/setup-web` writes one browser server into a project's `.mcp.json` today: `chrome-devtools`, which opens a Chrome window with one saved profile per project. The owner decides whether it also writes a second server, `chrome-devtools-headless`, which runs Chrome with no window in a fresh profile each run, and which flags that server takes.

`/setup-web` is the ok-web plugin's slash command that sets up the browser tools an agent uses in a web project. An entry in `.mcp.json` tells Claude Code which tool server to start. Chrome lets one process hold a profile at a time, so two sessions in the same project contend for the one headed browser; [step 5 of the skill](plugins/ok-web/skills/setup-web/SKILL.md#L95-L100) tells the owner that only one can hold it. A headless server started with `--isolated` takes a new profile each run, so it never contends and never opens a window on the owner's screen. The skill's [opening](plugins/ok-web/skills/setup-web/SKILL.md#L16-L20) says the suite adds new web-project servers to this command, each under the same rule: merge into the file, and never overwrite an entry the owner changed.

The verantel project carries both servers in a hand-written `.mcp.json`. Its headless entry adds `--chrome-arg=--host-resolver-rules=MAP *.test 127.0.0.1`, which maps that project's own test hostnames; a shared entry leaves that to each project. A project set up with `/setup-web`, such as zonebase, gets only the headed server. The owner wants both. No concept, story, or decision covers `/setup-web`. The [surface intent](.ok-planner/surface/surface.md#L31) makes it a public slash command, so a new entry changes what a public command writes.

The ruling decides which servers `/setup-web` writes by default, and the headless server's flags.

recommendation.text:
`/setup-web` writes both servers by default: the headed `chrome-devtools` server as it stands, and a `chrome-devtools-headless` server with `--headless --isolated` and no other flag. Each entry follows the same merge rules: add it where its key is missing, leave it where it matches, and show both versions where the owner's entry differs. The report says to use the headless server for unattended work and for a second session in the same project, and the headed server where the owner needs to watch the browser or log in. Project-specific Chrome arguments, such as host-resolver rules, stay with each project.

Rationale: option A gives every web project the fix for the contention the skill's own report names as its limit, and the skill already commits to adding web-project servers under its merge rules. The owner's stated want is both. Option B hides the fix behind an argument a new project would not know to pass, and option C leaves the contention in place. The cost of option A is one more server for each project to approve, paid once. The flip case: if the headless server's tool list costs enough context in every session that most projects would never use it, option B serves better.

problem.after:
`review certified`, the command that decides whether a sprint is done, fails a sprint when a deferred product-slow verdict has no open issue that names its site. Once a later sprint closes that issue as promoted, the issue is no longer open, so a rerun on the first sprint reports it not complete though nothing in it changed. The owner decides which issues count.

A product-slow verdict says a test is slow because the product code it runs is slow. Where the latest whole-suite round leaves nothing else to fix, certification defers the verdict and files it as an issue for the next sprint, per [decision:product-slow-fixes-ride-a-round-that-runs-anyway](.ok-planner/design/decisions/product-slow-fixes-ride-a-round-that-runs-anyway.md). `/plan-sprint` promotes an issue and leaves it open; that sprint's archive step closes it as promoted and moves it to the archive of closed issues ([plan-sprint SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L248)). [review:unfiled_deferred](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L2224-L2234) reads issues through [issues:select](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L684-L697), which returns open issues only. `review certified` skips the check for an archived sprint ([review](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L2283)). So the false failure needs a sprint left unarchived while a later sprint promotes and closes its verdict's issue.

The most recent sprint's certification added the check. Its fixer counted open issues only, as the [owner list](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/owner-list.md) skips a site an open issue already names. [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) asks that done mean the same thing for every sprint.

recommendation.text:
For a project with no recorded test, both the test preflight and `/ok-setup`'s runner check run setup twice and check that each run exits 0, and run setup beside a scratch resource and check that it exits 0 and the resource still stands. Each skips only the readiness half, which needs a recorded test to pass, and says so in one line. The decision on the three suite checks states this case, so the two sites cannot drift apart again.

Rationale: the decision commits both sites to the same checks, and option C keeps them the same while keeping the checks that cost minutes and need no test. A setup that fails on a second run, or that stops on resources the owner started, are faults the decision's rationale names, and a fresh project meets them in its first sprint, before any test exists. Option A keeps those checks in the preflight alone, so the owner who sets testing up meets the faults later. Option B drops them from both sites, and a fresh project then pays a whole-suite round for each fault. The flip case: if a stack often cannot start before the first test task writes files it needs, the partial checks fail where setup is not at fault, and option B serves better.

problem.after:
The task tracker lets a task start once every task it waits on has closed, even one that stopped short. So a sprint's build stage can start on top of unfinished work. The owner decides whether a task that closes short still frees the tasks waiting on it.

The task tracker (`.ok-planner/bin/tasks`) records one run's tasks. An agent closes its task `done`, or `partial` or `blocked` when it stops short. [tasks:open_waits](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L807-L813) counts a wait open only while the waited-on task is not closed. The drain loop, which starts an agent on each ready task, does not judge an outcome ([drain.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_tasks/drain.md#L250)). Sprint execution refiles a short stage as a new task only after the drain reports back ([sprint execution](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L472-L474)). The refile joins the waits of each waiter not yet claimed ([tasks:cmd_refile](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tasks#L1060-L1085)), so it misses a claimed one.

On 2026-11-12 this happened three times, each waiter claimed within 11 seconds of the partial close.

`/converge` relies on the current rule. Its fixers run in chains and its confirm drivers in relays, each task waiting on the one before. A fixer that closes `partial` passes its defects to the next round with no refile, and a blocked driver is never refiled. A rule that frees waiters only on `done` stalls both.

The ruling decides what the tracker owes a task that waits on one that closed short.

problem:
Two `/converge` prompts say a fixer always follows a verdict that blames the product for a slow test, but a design decision files that fix only beside another test failure. An agent that follows the prompts expects a fix that may never come.

A speed reader and a test verifier are agents that read a slow test for wasted time. Either can record a product-slow verdict: the test is slow because the product code it runs is slow. [decision:product-slow-fixes-ride-a-round-that-runs-anyway](.ok-planner/design/decisions/product-slow-fixes-ride-a-round-that-runs-anyway.md) commits sprint certification to apply that fix only beside another failure of the latest whole-suite round. It sends each other verdict to the intake for the next sprint. The shared sprint text states this condition. The test-speed and test-verify prompts do not.

A fixer noticed this outside its brief, and no merge agent checked it. On 2026-11-12 both prompts still read as filed.

Site: [test-speed.md:Record](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-speed.md#L108-L110) and [test-verify.md:A test](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-verify.md#L76-L78). Entry: [A8](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L16), a commitment of a live artifact under `.ok-planner/design/` leaves one compliant form. Trigger: a speed reader or test verifier records a product-slow verdict where the latest whole-suite round lists no other failure. Evidence: [test-speed.md:108](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-speed.md#L108) 'the fix loop files a fixer for the site, keyed `perf:`, and once the fix is accepted the test gets a fresh speed read'; [test-verify.md:77](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-verify.md#L77) 'the fix loop files a fixer for the site, keyed `perf:`, and once the fix is accepted the test gets a fresh speed read'; the sibling [_sprint/shared.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_sprint/shared.md#L866-L870) 'the fix loop files a fixer for the site, keyed `perf:`, beside another failure of the latest whole-suite round ... A verdict with no such failure beside it goes to the intake for the next sprint.'

recommendation.text: Fix [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-speed.md:Record](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-speed.md#L108-L110) and [plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-verify.md:A test](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-verify.md#L76-L78) so a product-slow verdict where no other failure of the latest whole-suite round stands is no longer described as filing a fixer.

title: Two `/converge` test prompts promise a slow-product fix with no condition

problem.after:
When a sprint opens test stages, the sprint template has the executing session run every code stage in step 4, but it creates the progress checklist only in step 6. A session that follows the steps in order lands every code stage before the checklist exists, so the owner watching the run sees no progress.

A sprint runs as stages, each one build task that an agent takes from the task tracker. The progress checklist is the harness task list, one entry per stage, that shows the owner which stages have landed; [story:watch-execution-progress](.ok-planner/design/stories/watch-execution-progress.md) promises that view. [decision:task-tools-mirror-the-report](.ok-planner/design/decisions/task-tools-mirror-the-report.md) says the session creates one entry per stage when it files the build tasks.

A run opens test stages where the sprint plans tests or the project's testing setting is on. Step 4 of the template's "How to execute this sprint" section files the build tasks, then files the test stages to wait on the code stages. It then tells the session to drain the tracker with step 7's loop, which runs every ready task. That drain runs every build task the test stages wait on. Step 6, which creates the checklist, comes later.

The decision gives the checklist a numbered step of its own because executors skipped it when it trailed the report step: a measured run under that form started its first three agents with no checklist. The current order lets that failure recur.

A drive of story watch-execution-progress during the certification of the eighth intake-drain sprint found this, and a merge agent confirmed it.

problem.after:
The `/converge` verifier prompt accepts a declined fix for three reasons and leaves out a fourth that the fixer prompt requires: the fix would change a behavior a user across a release boundary sees, and no ruling allows it. A verifier that follows the prompt sends such a decline back until the defect sticks. The owner then gets a stuck defect, its code restored and its fix rounds spent, where the skill meant to hand over a question.

A release boundary separates code that ships in one release from a user that does not update in the same step. The fixer prompt tells a fixer to decline a fix that must change what such a user sees and to record a question, because that change is the owner's to rule on. The verifier prompt accepts a decline only where the defect is not real, the project's accept list of harms leaves it standing, or the fix lies only in a file the run leaves alone. A boundary decline meets none of the three, so the verifier sends it back. At the run's limit of send-backs the defect is stuck: a restorer returns its code to its earlier behavior, and the defect reaches the owner as a stuck judgment issue. The prompt that files a run's leftovers already turns a verified boundary decline into a judgment issue, so the three prompts disagree.

A drive of [story:find-and-fix-defects](.ok-planner/design/stories/find-and-fix-defects.md) in the most recent sprint's certification found this, and a second agent confirmed it.

problem.before:
The `/converge` verifier prompt lists the reasons a verifier accepts a declined defect, and leaves out the one reason the fixer prompt requires: a fix that would change a behavior a user across a release boundary observes, with no ruling that allows it. A verifier that follows the text sends that decline back until the defect sticks, so the owner running `/converge` gets a stuck defect, with its code restored and fix rounds spent, where the skill meant to hand over a boundary question.

In `/converge`, a fixer fixes one defect at a time, and a verifier then reads only the fixer's change and each decline's reason. A release boundary separates code that ships in one release from a user that does not update in the same step. The fixer prompt tells a fixer to decline a fix that must change such a behavior and to record a question, because that change is the owner's to rule on. The verifier prompt accepts a decline only where the defect is not real, the accept list leaves it standing, or the fix lies only in a file the run leaves alone. A boundary-question decline is none of the three, so the verifier sends it back. Each send-back raises the defect's count; at the run's limit the defect is stuck, a restorer returns its code to its prior behavior, and the owner list files it as a stuck judgment issue. The owner-list prompt already routes a verified boundary-question decline into a judgment issue of its own, so the skill's three prompts disagree.

A drive of story [story:find-and-fix-defects](.ok-planner/design/stories/find-and-fix-defects.md) in the certification of the eighth intake-drain sprint found this, and a merge agent confirmed it; the three texts stood the same at that sprint's base.
